stages.name: Developing primary industries
stages.title: Developing primary industries
stages.sub: Why some poor countries choose to build up farming, mining and other primary industries, and what they gain from it.

steps.q: A country relies heavily on exporting one or two raw materials, like copper or coffee, and little else. What is it sitting on, that it has not yet used to the full?
steps.right: A large stock of untapped natural resources
steps.wrong: A large stock of finished manufactured goods
steps.hint: Copper and coffee both start out as raw materials in the ground or in the soil.
steps.pre: So the country has a big untapped

steps.q: To turn more of that copper ore or farmland into exports, what does the country need to put in first: roads, machinery, irrigation, mining equipment?
steps.right: Money spent on getting more out of the ground and land
steps.wrong: Money spent on advertising the country abroad
steps.hint: Digging deeper mines or farming more land both need equipment and infrastructure before any extra output appears.

steps.q: A government decides to pour funding into mining, farming and fishing rather than into building factories or call centres. What is it choosing to expand?
steps.hint: Mining, farming and fishing all produce raw materials, not finished goods or services.

steps.q: As mines and farms expand, more workers are hired and more raw materials are sold abroad. Does the country gain anything from this, even while still depending on primary products?
steps.right: Yes, more jobs and export earnings
steps.wrong: No, no jobs or export earnings
steps.hint: Think about what happens to employment and to money coming in from abroad as the sector grows.
